lead: A stiffened panel is a skin with stringers running along the load. In compression the thin skin buckles between the stringers long before the stringers fail. The buckled skin still works, but mostly in narrow strips next to each stringer. The effective width method replaces the real, uneven stress in the skin by a strip of width b<sub>e</sub> working at the stringer stress. Wing upper surfaces, fuselage crowns and tail compression skins are sized this way, and the stringer with its effective skin becomes the boom of the idealised section.
prereq: You need: the plate buckling stress σcr = kπ²E(t/b)²/[12(1 − ν²)] from buckling of thin plates.

sections.h3: Sheets and stiffened panels under compression

blocks.text: A flat sheet alone is a poor compression member: its buckling stress varies as (t/b)², so a wide thin sheet buckles at a few MPa. Stringers riveted or bonded to it at a pitch p divide it into narrow bays, each a plate supported along the stringer lines, and the sheet buckling stress rises to σ<sub>cr</sub> = kπ²E(t/p)²/[12(1 − ν²)], with k = 4 if the stringer lines are taken as simple supports.

Above σ<sub>cr</sub> the middle of each bay bows out of plane and stops taking extra load. The sheet next to each stringer is held straight by it and keeps straining with it, so its stress keeps rising with the stringer stress σ<sub>s</sub>. Across a bay the stress is therefore high at the stringers and low at mid-bay. The panel fails only when the stringers fail, by crippling or as columns between ribs. This is why a stiffened panel is much lighter than an unstiffened sheet that carries the same compressive load.

Von Kármán replaced the uneven stress by two strips of sheet, one each side of the stringer, working at the full stringer stress σ<sub>s</sub>, with the rest of the bay carrying nothing. He sized the strips by asking how wide a simply supported plate could be and still be on the point of buckling at σ<sub>s</sub>. Setting 4π²E(t/b<sub>e</sub>)²/[12(1 − ν²)] = σ<sub>s</sub> and solving for b<sub>e</sub>:

blocks.where: b<sub>e</sub> is the total effective width of sheet working with one stringer, half on each side (mm); t the sheet thickness (mm); E Young's modulus and σ<sub>s</sub> the stringer stress, in the same unit; the 1.90 is for ν = 0.3.

blocks.text: As σ<sub>s</sub> rises, b<sub>e</sub> shrinks: the more the panel is loaded, the more the sheet sheds load to the stringers. The formula only applies once the sheet has buckled. When b<sub>e</sub> from it is larger than the pitch p, the stress is below σ<sub>cr</sub> and the whole bay is effective. The stringer and its effective sheet form one effective area, and the panel load per stringer follows:
A<sub>e</sub> = A<sub>st</sub> + b<sub>e</sub> t,   P = σ<sub>s</sub> A<sub>e</sub>
blocks.where: A<sub>e</sub> is the effective area per stringer (mm²); A<sub>st</sub> the stringer area (mm²); P the load carried by one stringer and its sheet (N).

items: Find the stringer stress σ<sub>s</sub> for the load case.
Check whether the sheet has buckled: compare σ<sub>s</sub> with σ<sub>cr</sub> of a bay of width p.
If it has, compute b<sub>e</sub> = 1.90 t √(E/σ<sub>s</sub>), and take b<sub>e</sub> = p if the formula gives more.
Add the effective sheet to the stringer: A<sub>e</sub> = A<sub>st</sub> + b<sub>e</sub> t.
Use A<sub>e</sub> as the boom area in the idealised section, and check the stringer for crippling and for column buckling between ribs.

sections.h3: Limits of the method and shear lag

blocks.text: The 1.90 assumes the stringers hold the bay edges straight and give simple support. Riveted stringers with some rotational restraint give a little more; test-based coefficients are used in design offices. The method also assumes the stringer does not cripple first, so the local strength of the stringer must be checked separately.

Shear lag is a second reason why a wide skin is not fully effective, and it happens even without buckling. In a box beam the bending load enters the skins from the spar webs as shear. The skin strains in shear as it passes the load inwards, so the direct stress is highest next to the webs and falls towards the middle of the skin, instead of being uniform as simple bending theory assumes. Stringer loads then build up over a length along the span instead of at once. Shear lag matters most for wide, short boxes, near wing roots, at cut-outs and where concentrated loads are fed in, and it is handled with an effective width of skin in the same spirit.

figure.caption: The worked panel at a stringer stress of 100 MPa. The real skin stress (shaded curve) stays at 100 MPa at each stringer and falls towards the bay buckling stress of 25.3 MPa at mid-bay. Von Kármán's effective width replaces it by strips totalling b<sub>e</sub> = 75.4 mm per stringer, 37.7 mm each side, at the full 100 MPa, so A<sub>e</sub> = 313.1 mm².

spec.aria: A row of four stringers 150 millimetres apart under a skin line. Above the skin, a shaded curve of skin stress rises to 100 megapascals at each stringer and dips at mid-bay towards a dashed line at 25.3 megapascals, the buckling stress of a bay. Rectangles centred on each stringer, 75.4 millimetres wide in total and 100 megapascals high, show the effective width. Labels give b e of 75.4 millimetres, 37.7 each side, and the effective area of 313.1 square millimetres.

examples.question: A compression panel has stringers of area 200 mm² at a pitch of 150 mm on a 1.5 mm skin, with E = 70 GPa and ν = 0.3. Find the stress at which the skin bays buckle. When the stringer stress is 100 MPa, find the effective width, the effective area and the load per stringer, and compare with a skin that did not buckle.
steps: At σ<sub>s</sub> = 100 MPa the sheet has buckled, since 100 > 25.3.
E/σ<sub>s</sub> = 70,000/100 = 700, √700 = 26.46. b<sub>e</sub> = 1.90 × 1.5 × 26.46 = 75.4 mm, 37.7 mm each side of the stringer; it is less than p = 150 mm, so the formula applies.
Load per stringer: P = 100 × 313.1 = 31,311 N = 31.3 kN; the sheet carries 11.3 kN of it.
Average sheet stress over the bay: 100 × 75.4/150 = 50.3 MPa, against 100 MPa at the stringer.
If the sheet had not buckled, the whole 150 mm would work: A = 200 + 225 = 425 mm² and P = 42.5 kN. Buckling costs 26% of the load at this stress.
examples.answer: σ<sub>cr</sub> = 25.3 MPa; at 100 MPa, b<sub>e</sub> = 75.4 mm (37.7 mm each side), A<sub>e</sub> = 313.1 mm² and P = 31.3 kN per stringer.

examples.question: The stringers of the same panel cripple at 250 MPa. The panel is 1200 mm wide with 8 stringers. Find the effective width at failure and the failing load of the panel, ignoring column buckling between ribs.
steps: b<sub>e</sub> = 1.90 × 1.5 × √(70,000/250) = 2.85 × 16.73 = 47.7 mm, less than the pitch, so the sheet is buckled.
Check against the loaded skin: the whole cross-section is 8 × 200 + 1200 × 1.5 = 3,400 mm², so the average failing stress is 160 MPa, well below the 250 MPa in the stringers.
examples.answer: b<sub>e</sub> = 47.7 mm at failure; the panel fails at about 543 kN (67.9 kN per stringer).

traps: Taking 1.90 t √(E/σ) as the width on each side. It is the total width working with one stringer; each side gets half.
Using the effective width formula before the sheet has buckled, or keeping b<sub>e</sub> larger than the pitch. Below σ<sub>cr</sub>, or when b<sub>e</sub> > p, the whole bay is effective.
Using the yield stress, or the sheet buckling stress, for σ in the formula. Use the stringer stress at the load case being checked.
Mixing units inside √(E/σ). E and σ must be in the same unit; b<sub>e</sub> comes out in the unit of t.
Thinking shear lag needs buckling. Shear lag reduces skin effectiveness in an unbuckled box near roots and cut-outs, through shear strain in the skin.

quiz.a: The width of sheet which, working at the full stringer stress, carries the same load as the real buckled sheet with its uneven stress.

quiz.q: Why does the middle of a buckled bay carry little extra load while the sheet next to a stringer carries a lot?
quiz.a: The middle bows out of plane, so compressing it further mostly increases the bow. The sheet next to the stringer is held straight and strains with the stringer, so its stress rises with the stringer stress.

quiz.q: A sheet has t = 2 mm, E = 72 GPa and a stringer stress of 120 MPa. Find the total effective width and the width each side of the stringer.
For the same sheet the pitch is 80 mm. Is the formula valid? What effective area goes with a 250 mm² stringer?
quiz.a: b<sub>e</sub> = 93.1 mm exceeds p = 80 mm, so the stress is below the sheet buckling stress and the whole bay is effective: A<sub>e</sub> = 250 + 80 × 2 = 410 mm².

quiz.q: As a panel is loaded from σ<sub>cr</sub> up to stringer failure, how does the share of load taken by the sheet change? Use the formula to explain.
quiz.a: b<sub>e</sub> = 1.90 t √(E/σ<sub>s</sub>) falls as σ<sub>s</sub> rises, while the stringer load rises in proportion to σ<sub>s</sub>. The sheet load σ<sub>s</sub> b<sub>e</sub> t grows only as √σ<sub>s</sub>, so the stringer takes a growing share as the load increases.

quiz.q: Explain shear lag in a wide box beam and where it matters on a wing.
quiz.a: Bending load enters the skins from the spar webs as shear; the skin deforms in shear as it carries load inwards, so the direct stress is highest at the webs and lower mid-panel. Simple bending theory overestimates the skin's share. It matters at wing roots, near cut-outs and at concentrated load inputs, where loads change quickly along the span.

beyond: Not for the exam. Effective width formulas with test coefficients (Winter's formula for cold-formed steel is one) are used across structures. Post-buckled stiffened panels are now checked with nonlinear finite element models, and composite panels are often designed to work post-buckled with care for skin–stringer separation. Search for von Kármán effective width and shear lag in box beams.
